q: A white wine bright at bottling turns cloudy after an afternoon in a hot car, although nothing has spoiled. Which treatment before bottling prevents that?
opts: A warmer bottling temperature, which keeps the proteins dissolved
A bentonite clay fining, which takes the proteins out
A heavier dose of sulphur dioxide just before bottling
A longer spell on the sediment, which settles the proteins out
exp: Grape proteins stay dissolved while a wine is cool and come out of solution when it is warmed, which is why the haze appears in transit or on a shelf and never in the cellar. Bentonite is a swelling clay that binds those proteins and is filtered away with them, and it is standard insurance on nearly every commercial white.

q: Held at minus four degrees for a week before bottling, a white throws a crust on the tank wall which is then filtered away. What has been prevented?
opts: Crystals appearing in the bottle later on
The wine browning on the shop shelf
A protein haze in warm weather
A refermentation in the bottle later on
exp: Potassium bitartrate is far less soluble in cold wine, so chilling forces it out where it can be removed rather than leaving it to appear on a cold shelf months later. More producers skip the step each year, on the grounds that the deposit is a cosmetic matter and the chilling costs the wine some aroma.

q: Two filters stand in the bottling room: one traps particles inside a thick pad of medium, the other has a rated pore size that nothing larger can pass. Which one alone can be relied on to hold a sweet wine stable in bottle, and why?
opts: The pad, because it feeds the wine a little oxygen too
The rated membrane, because it lowers the wine's alcohol
The pad, because it takes far more solids out in a single pass
The rated membrane, because it removes every live yeast cell
exp: A sweet wine is a bottle of food for any yeast that survives bottling, and a membrane rated below a micron is the usual guarantee against that. The pad is cheaper and gentler and takes the bulk of the solids out first, so the two are run in sequence rather than as rivals.

q: A guest asks whether a wine is suitable for a vegan diet. Which stage of production is the reason the answer is sometimes no?
opts: Filtration, because the pads themselves are made from gelatin
Bottling, because the capsules are sealed with wax from animals
Fermentation, because yeast is counted as an animal product
Fining, because several fining agents are animal-derived
exp: Gelatin, isinglass from fish swim bladders, casein from milk and beaten egg white have all been used for centuries, and little or none of them normally survives into the bottle, though milk and egg agents must still be declared on an EU label unless the residue is shown to fall below the legal limit. The vegan question turns on whether an animal product was used at all rather than on what is left behind, so producers making the claim switch to mineral or plant-based agents, or bottle without fining.

q: Nothing is fined out of a wine and nothing is filtered before it is bottled. What is being traded, and for what?
opts: Some clarity and stability, in return for texture and aroma
Some colour, in return for a longer life in bottle
Some alcohol, in return for a longer finish and a fuller body
Some acidity, in return for a softer palate at the table
exp: Every fining and every filtration removes something besides its target, and the argument for leaving a wine alone is that the collateral loss outweighs the gain. The price is a wine that may throw a deposit and is less predictable in transit, which is a real consideration on a long shipping route.

q: The last and hardest fraction to come out of a red press is run into its own tank, apart from the wine that drained off under gravity. Why keep them separate?
opts: It is sweeter than the free-run wine, since the skins give up sugar
It is paler and softer than the free-run, so it is sold off in bulk
It is cloudier than free-run wine, so it is always discarded
It is darker, more tannic and coarser, so how much goes back is a choice
exp: Free-run wine is the elegant part, while press wine carries structure and colour that a blend may badly need in a light year. The fractions are tasted separately and a proportion is folded back in, or none at all.

q: Grapes are squeezed slowly through a deep cake of skins in a vertical basket rather than driven along by a continuous screw. What does the slower press give?
opts: Cleaner juice with less bitterness, since the cake filters it
A far higher yield per tonne, since the cake gives the plate more to press
Juice carrying more colour and tannin than a continuous press gives
A faster turnaround at harvest, since the basket empties itself
exp: Hard, fast pressing tears skins and cracks pips and drives phenolics and solids into the juice, and no later treatment fully undoes it. The basket press is slow and labour-hungry, which is why it survives at the quality end and almost nowhere else.

q: Twenty small lots ferment separately in one cellar when a single large tank would have been far cheaper to fill and to clean. What does that buy?
opts: Each parcel can be judged and treated on its own
The wine ferments faster in small volumes than in large ones
The wine reaches a higher alcohol in a small vessel
Small lots need no filtration before bottling
exp: Blending is a subtractive art as much as an additive one, and keeping lots apart is what makes leaving something out possible at all. Once a spoiled barrel has gone into the tank there is no way back, which is the whole argument for the extra work.

q: A tech sheet records a cuvaison of twenty-one days. Which part of the process does that figure describe?
opts: The time the wine spent in barrel afterwards
The time the wine spent in contact with the skins
The time the wine spent on its own sediment
The time between bottling and release to the trade
exp: The figure covers the whole span in the fermenting vessel with the solids, taking in any cold soak beforehand and any maceration after the sugar has gone. A number well beyond the length of the ferment itself is therefore a signal that the cellar macerated afterwards.

q: A grower says the wine will not be bottled for eighteen months, during which it will be racked, topped up, blended and fined. Which single French word covers that whole span?
opts: Assemblage
Mutage
Soutirage
Elevage
exp: The word means raising or bringing up, and it takes in maturation, movement, blending and clarification alike. It says nothing on its own about the vessel, so eighteen months of it may mean steel, concrete, clay or oak in any combination.

q: Argue the Trimbach position on grand cru labeling in one sentence.
accept: house name over cru brand consistency
brands trump crus clos sainte hune exception
ans: The house holds that its names (Clos Sainte-Hune, Frédéric Émile) guarantee more than the cru system's politics — so the labels omit 'grand cru'
exp: Master orals ask you to argue producers' philosophies, not just recite.

q: Name the third Alsace wine AOP beside Alsace and Alsace Grand Cru.
ans: Crémant d'Alsace (and, structurally, the 51 individual Grand Cru AOPs since 2011)
exp: Three historic AOPs; the crus' independence made it 53 by legal count.

q: Which grand cru's name means 'sorcerers' hill', beloved of Gewurztraminer at Zind-Humbrecht?
accept: hexenberg no sorcerer goldert brand hengst
ans: (The trap: 'Hexenbückel' is folklore) — accept discussion; Hengst = stallion, Goldert = golden slope: etymologies are oral fodder
exp: Master examiners play etymology games; compose, don't freeze.

ans: Savagnin Rose (non-aromatic Traminer) around Heiligenstein — a protected local relic
exp: Klevner — no second 'e' — means Pinot Blanc, while Klevener de Heiligenstein is Savagnin Rose. One letter apart.

q: The medieval Ammerschwihr wine fraternity, revived in 1947 and now seated at the Château de Kientzheim, is called:
ans: The Confrérie Saint-Étienne (seal-tastings and the sigillé label)
exp: Its library cellar reaches back to 1834 — orals adore living history.

q: Which producer's 'Clos Windsbuhl' and 'Clos Jebsal' bottlings map Pinot Gris' range?
ans: Zind-Humbrecht (Windsbuhl: limestone freshness; Jebsal: marl-gypsum richness/SGN)
exp: Olivier Humbrecht MW pioneered the indice sweetness scale for their labels.
